title: Core Vocabulary

learn.summary: Word frequency follows Zipf's law: a tiny core does almost all the work. Roughly the 1000 most frequent word families cover about 85% of everyday speech; the first 100 words alone cover close to half. So learn by frequency, not by textbook theme — 'because', 'maybe', and 'want' beat 'giraffe' and 'briefcase' every day of the week.

do: Learn the 100 most frequent words of your target language this week using a frequency list, 20 per day.

children.title: Frequency Lists

learn.summary: A frequency list ranks words by how often they occur in a large corpus of real text or subtitles. Subtitle-based lists best match conversation; newspaper corpora skew formal. Use the list as your syllabus for the first 1000-2000 words, then let your own reading and listening take over as the source of new vocabulary.

do: Find a subtitle-based frequency list for your language and import the top 500 words into your flashcard app.

children.title: The First 500

learn.summary: Your first 500 words should be function words (and, but, if, very), core verbs (go, want, have, can, make), question words, numbers, and the pronouns — the skeleton every sentence hangs on. Learn words inside short example sentences, not as isolated translations; context is what makes them retrievable in conversation. Aim for recognition first, production second.

do: For each of 15 new words per day, write or copy one short example sentence and learn the sentence, not the bare word.

children.title: Cognates & False Friends

learn.summary: Cognates are free vocabulary: an English speaker starting Spanish already 'knows' thousands of -tion/-ción and -ty/-dad words. But false friends bite — Spanish 'embarazada' means pregnant, German 'Gift' means poison, French 'librairie' is a bookshop. Harvest cognate patterns systematically in week one, and keep a short blacklist of the famous traps.

do: Write down 3 cognate transformation rules for your language pair and the 10 most notorious false friends.

children.title: Spaced Repetition & Anki

learn.summary: Hermann Ebbinghaus mapped the forgetting curve in 1885: memories decay exponentially unless refreshed, and each well-timed review flattens the curve. Spaced-repetition software like Anki schedules reviews at exactly those expanding intervals, making 20-30 new words a day sustainable at about 15-20 minutes of daily review. The rule that matters: never skip review days, and delete cards that bore you.

do: Install Anki, add 15 new cards daily for 7 straight days, and clear your review queue every single day.
